extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners (attorneys/agents) handling restriction and double-patenting issues
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for making and responding to restriction requirements (including special rules for nucleotide sequences) and for analyzing/issuing statutory and nonstatutory double patenting rejections, including provisional rejections and terminal disclaimer practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Election and fee or petition under transitional restriction provisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant must either: (1) elect the invention or inventions to be searched and examined and pay the fee set forth in 37 CFR 1.17(s) for each independent and distinct invention in excess of one which applicant elects; or (2) file a petition under 37 CFR 1.129(b) traversing the requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this form paragraph in restriction/election requirements for applications subject to transition restriction provisions (mailed after June 8, 1995). Procedure NOT applicable to design or reissue applications. See current fee schedule for proper amount.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refund when divided inventions rejoined by linking claim allowance
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever divided inventions in a transitional application are rejoined because a linking claim is allowable and applicant paid the fee set forth in 37 CFR 1.17(s) for the additional invention, applicant should be notified that he or she may request a refund of the fee paid for that additional invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies where rejoining occurs due to an allowable linking claim (see MPEP §§ 809, 821.04). Examiner should notify applicant of refund availability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refund when nonelected species embraced by allowable generic claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever claims drawn to an additional species in a transitional application for which applicant paid the fee in 37 CFR 1.17(s) are no longer withdrawn from consideration because they are fully embraced by an allowable generic claim, applicant should be notified that he or she may request a refund of the fee paid for that additional species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determination of when claims to a nonelected species would no longer be withdrawn should be made as indicated in MPEP §§ 806.04(d), 821.04, and 821.04(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Nucleotide sequences presumed independent and distinct (general rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Polynucleotide molecules defined by their nucleic acid that encode different proteins are structurally distinct chemical compounds; these sequences are thus deemed to normally constitute independent and distinct inventions within the meaning of 35 U.S.C. 121.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absent evidence to the contrary, each such nucleotide sequence is presumed to represent an independent and distinct invention and be subject to a restriction requirement pursuant to 35 U.S.C. 121 and 37 CFR 1.141 et seq.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial waiver: reasonable number of nucleotide sequences (ten)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Director has sua sponte partially waived the requirements of 37 CFR 1.141 et seq. and permitted a reasonable number of nucleotide sequences to be claimed in a single application; it has been determined that normally ten sequences constitute a reasonable number for examination purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accordingly, in most cases, up to ten independent and distinct nucleotide sequences will be examined in a single application without restriction. Exceptional cases (complex claims) may require fewer than ten. Applicants may petition under 37 CFR 1.181 for examination of additional sequences by providing evidence that the different nucleotide sequences do not cover independent and distinct inventions. See MPEP §1850 for PCT/national stage treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentably indistinct sequences examined with selected sequences
rubrics_metrics.description: In addition to the specifically selected sequences, those sequences which are patentably indistinct from the selected sequences will also be examined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applicant selects sequences for examination, any claim elements patentably indistinct from those sequences are also to be examined and may be rejoined/allowed as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sequences encoding same protein examined together (not independent/distinct)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nucleotide sequences encoding the same protein are not considered to be independent and distinct inventions and will continue to be examined together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If sequences encode the same protein, they are treated as patentably indistinct for restriction purposes; they do not count separately toward the ten-sequence guideline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of claims in alternative form to many individual sequences (example A)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications claiming more than ten individual independent and distinct nucleotide sequences in alternative form (e.g., 'an isolated and purified DNA fragment comprising DNA having at least 95% identity to a DNA sequence selected from SEQ ID Nos. 1-1,000') will be subject to a restriction requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only the ten nucleotide sequences selected in response to the requirement and any other claimed restriction sequences which are patentably indistinct therefrom will be examined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of combination claims of sequences (example B)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications claiming only a combination of nucleotide sequences (e.g., a combination comprising SEQ ID Nos. 1-1,000) will generally not be subject to a restriction requirement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presence of one novel and nonobvious sequence within the combination will render the entire combination allowable. The combination will be searched until one nucleotide sequence is found to be allowable. The examiner selects the order of searching to maximize identification of an allowable sequence; if no individual sequence is found allowable, the examiner will consider whether the combination as a whole renders the claim allowable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of composition claims reciting different combinations (example C)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications claiming compositions reciting different combinations of individual nucleotide sequences (example C) will be subject to a restriction requirement; applicants will be required to select one combination for examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the selected combination contains ten or fewer sequences, all sequences of the combination will be searched. If the selected combination contains more than ten sequences, the combination will be examined following the procedures for example B (search until one sequence is found allowable, examiner chooses order to maximize allowance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure when application contains multiple claim types (A–C)
rubrics_metrics.description: In applications containing all three claim types (A–C), the Office will require restriction of the application to ten sequences for initial examination purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Based upon finding allowable sequences, claims limited to the allowable sequences (example A), all combinations (B and C) containing the allowable sequences and any patentably indistinct sequences will be rejoined and allowed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejoinder consideration for nonelected claims requiring allowable nucleotide sequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Nonelected claims requiring any allowable nucleotide sequence(s) should be considered for rejoinder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a nonelected claim depends upon or requires an allowable nucleotide sequence, examiner should consider rejoining those nonelected claims (see MPEP §821.04).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and public-policy basis of double patenting
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine of double patenting seeks to prevent the unjustified extension of patent exclusivity beyond the term of a patent; double patenting results when the right to exclude granted by a first patent is unjustly extended by the grant of a later issued patent or patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The focus of any double patenting analysis is on the claims in the multiple patents or patent applications involved. For double patenting to be considered, two or more patents or applications must have at least one common inventor and/or be commonly assigned/owned or be subject to a proper joint research agreement (35 U.S.C. 103(c)(2) and (3)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Two types of double patenting rejections (statutory vs nonstatutory)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are generally two types of double patenting rejections: (1) 'same invention' statutory type based on 35 U.S.C. 101, and (2) 'nonstatutory-type' double patenting rejection (judicially created) grounded in public policy, primarily to prevent prolongation of patent term when later claims are not patentably distinguishable from earlier claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nonstatutory double patenting includes rejections based on one-way or two-way obviousness determinations (obviousness-type double patenting). Nonstatutory rejections cannot be based on mere 'domination' absent statutory or nonstatutory grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner's required determinations before making double patenting rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining whether a proper basis exists to enter a double patenting rejection, the examiner must determine: (A) whether a double patenting rejection is prohibited by the third sentence of 35 U.S.C. 121; (B) whether a statutory basis exists; and (C) whether a nonstatutory basis exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each determination must be made on the basis of all the facts in the application before the examiner. Use Charts I-A, I-B, II-A, and II-B to illustrate methodology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory double patenting test (35 U.S.C. 101 — 'same invention')
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutory double patenting asks: Is the same invention being claimed twice? 'Same invention' means identical subject matter. A reliable test is whether a claim in the application could be literally infringed without literally infringing a corresponding claim in the patent (In re Vogel).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If there exists an embodiment that falls within the scope of one claim but not the other, then identical subject matter is not defined by both claims and statutory double patenting does not exist. Example: 'halogen' vs 'chlorine' — not identical; '36 inches' vs '3 feet' — same invention. Statutory double patenting cannot be overcome by a terminal disclaimer; it can be overcome by canceling or amending conflicting claims so they are no longer coextensive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provisional double patenting rejections practice
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'provisional' double patenting rejection may be made where conflicting claims exist between copending applications or between an application and a published application, provided confidentiality is not violated. Provisional rejections alert applicant to potential double patenting if one application issues as a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make provisional rejection in each application as long as conflicting claims exist in more than one application unless that provisional rejection is the only rejection remaining in at least one application. Procedures vary depending on which application has other rejections remaining; see rules on withdrawing provisional ODP, requiring terminal disclaimers in later-filed applications, and special handling when applications filed same day or when three applications conflict (terminal disclaimers required in at least two). Use form paragraphs 8.32 for provisional rejections. Where provisional statutory double patenting is only rejection remaining, withdraw in earlier-filed app and permit issuance; maintain provisional rejection in other app to convert when that app issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminal disclaimer mechanics for nonstatutory obviousness-type double patenting
rubrics_metrics.description: For nonstatutory (ODP) double patenting, a terminal disclaimer may be required in the later-filed (or 'improvement') application before the ODP rejection can be withdrawn; an earlier-filed/base application may be allowed to issue without a terminal disclaimer if ODP is the only remaining rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If ODP rejections are the only rejections remaining in multiple applications, withdraw ODP in earlier-filed application to permit issue without terminal disclaimer; require terminal disclaimer in later-filed application. If both applications filed same day, determine base vs improvement; base can issue without disclaimer, improvement cannot. For three conflicting applications, terminal disclaimers must be filed in at least two to link all three applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between domination and double patenting
rubrics_metrics.description: Domination exists when a first patent or application has a broad/generic claim that fully encompasses an invention defined in a narrower claim in another patent/application; domination alone cannot support a double patenting rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although domination by itself is insufficient to support double patenting, its presence does not preclude double patenting if statutory or nonstatutory grounds otherwise exist. Cite In re Kaplan and In re Sarrett for guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double patenting in reexamination and effect of CREATE Act (35 U.S.C. 103(c))
rubrics_metrics.description: Double patenting issues may be raised in reexamination proceedings; double patenting may exist where the reference patent/application and the patent under reexamination have at least one inventor/common owner or result from activities within a joint research agreement under 35 U.S.C. 103(c)(2) and (3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the patent under reexamination was granted on or after Dec 10, 2004, double patenting may exist on the basis of joint research agreements if evidence of the agreement is of record. A double patenting rejection may NOT be made on this basis if the patent under reexamination issued before Dec 10, 2004. The prior art exclusion under 35 U.S.C. 103(c) cannot be used to overcome an obvious double patenting rejection. See MPEP §2258 for reexamination double patenting practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of form paragraphs for statutory double patenting (¶ 8.30, 8.31, 8.32)
rubrics_metrics.description: Form paragraph 8.30 is the heading for statutory (same invention) double patenting rejections; ¶8.31 is used to reject claim as claiming same invention as claim of prior U.S. patent; ¶8.32 is used for provisional 35 U.S.C. 101 double patenting rejections against copending applications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ¶8.30 must be used as a heading preceding statutory double patenting rejections. ¶8.31 is used only for earlier patents (not copending apps); ¶8.32 is used only for conflicting claims in copending applications. Refer to examiner notes for bracket insertions, when to use additional form paragraphs (e.g., 7.15, 7.19, 8.27), and other procedural specifics.
